unit.title: Install, terminate and connect electrical wiring systems

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: You must connect a new cable into a junction box on an existing lighting circuit. The circuit breaker has been switched off. What must you do before you touch any conductor?
options: Check that the room lights have gone off
Ask a co-worker whether the circuit is dead
Lock off, tag and prove dead with a checked tester
Ask the customer whether the circuit has been switched off

questions.stem: Your voltage tester shows no voltage on a circuit. You then check the tester on the proving unit, and it does not light. What does this mean?
options: The tester may be faulty, so the circuit is not proved dead
The circuit is dead, so you can start work straight away
The proving unit is faulty, so the circuit must be dead
The circuit is dead, but only the neutral is safe to touch

questions.stem: Which wiring system has single insulated cables drawn into a tube that is fixed to the building?
options: Sheathed cable clipped direct
Cable laid on a tray
Steel-armoured cable
A conduit system

questions.stem: Why is armoured cable often used for a buried supply to an outbuilding?
options: It is cheaper than any other type of cable
Its steel armour protects it from damage
It does not need any earth connection
It can be bent much tighter than other cable

questions.stem: A sheathed cable must pass through a timber joist. Where should the hole be drilled?
options: Just under the top edge, where floorboards are nailed
Through the bottom edge, as low down as you can
Anywhere at all, as long as the hole is big enough
Near the middle of its depth, away from nail paths

questions.stem: What mainly decides the size (cross-section) of a circuit's conductors?
options: The colour of the cable insulation
The length of the room that the circuit is in
The current the circuit must safely carry
The number of screws in each accessory

questions.stem: Why may a long cable run need a bigger cable than a short run with the same load?
options: Long cables are more likely to be stolen
To keep the voltage drop small enough
Long cables carry less current than short ones
To make the cable easier to pull into conduit

questions.stem: A water heater in a Jamaican home runs on 220 V. What supply does it need?
options: Its own 220 V circuit with a two-pole breaker
A 110 V outlet circuit that is shared with the kitchen
Any lighting circuit, as long as the switch is a big one
A heavy extension cord from the nearest wall outlet

questions.stem: Before pulling cables into a conduit, what should you check?
options: The conduit is complete, clean and free of burrs
The cables are all the same colour as each other
The conduit is full of water to help the cables slide
The cables have been cut shorter than the run

questions.stem: What is the right way to pull several cables into a conduit?
options: Pull them in one at a time, as hard as you can
Twist them tightly together before pulling them in
Pull them in together, fed in straight and untwisted
Push them in from both ends so they meet in the middle

questions.stem: The main switch of a distribution board is switched off. Which parts can still be live?
options: The outgoing terminals of every circuit breaker
The neutral bar and the earth bar only
Nothing at all, once the main switch is off
The incoming supply cables and their terminals

questions.stem: Sheathed cable is clipped along a wall. How should the clips be fixed?
options: Close together at the ends only, with none in the middle
Evenly spaced as the code says, with the cable straight
As few as possible, so that the cable is free to move
Tight enough to squash the cable flat a little bit

questions.stem: Where a cable passes through a hole in a metal box, what must be fitted?
options: A cable tie around the cable
A strip of masking tape
A grommet or bush
A dab of grease on the edge

questions.stem: Why must a PVC-insulated cable not be run touching a hot water pipe?
options: The cable makes the water too cold
Heat can soften and damage the insulation
The pipe will rust where the cable touches it
The cable will make the pipe live at all times

questions.stem: Why must cables not be bent too sharply?
options: Sharp bends make the cable look untidy only
Sharp bends make the cable carry more current
Sharp bends change the colour of the conductor
Sharp bends can crack the insulation

questions.stem: When you strip the outer sheath of a cable, what must you take care not to do?
options: Cut or nick the insulation of the cores inside
Leave the sheath on just inside the box or enclosure
Use a cable stripper made for the job
Measure the length to strip before you start

questions.stem: How much insulation should be stripped from a conductor going into a screw terminal?
options: As much as you can, so there is plenty of bare copper showing
Just enough for the terminal, with no bare copper showing
None at all, because the terminal screw cuts through it
About 50 mm, so that the bare end can be folded back twice

questions.stem: Which tool is best for removing the insulation from a single core without damaging the copper?
options: A sharp knife pulled around the core several times
Your teeth, as they give a good grip on the plastic
Side cutters squeezed hard around the insulation
A wire stripper set to the conductor size

questions.stem: What is a crimp lug (cable lug) used for?
options: To join a cable to the outside of a metal conduit
To fix a cable firmly to the wall or ceiling
To end a conductor so it can be bolted to a terminal
To mark a cable with its circuit number and name

questions.stem: Why must the crimp tool and its die match the size of the lug?
options: So the crimp grips the conductor fully
So that the lug comes out in the correct colour
So that the crimp can be undone easily by hand later
So that the tool does not need to be squeezed fully

questions.stem: After tightening a screw terminal, how can you check that the conductor is held firmly?
options: Give the conductor a gentle tug
Switch on the circuit and watch for sparks
Tap the terminal hard with a hammer
Look at it from a distance of 2 m

questions.stem: Why should terminals be tightened to the maker's torque (tightness)?
options: So the screws can be taken out more easily later
Loose terminals can overheat; too tight can damage them
So the conductor can move freely inside the terminal
So the accessory can be fitted without a box

questions.stem: In a lamp holder with a screw (Edison) base, which conductor goes to the centre contact?
options: The neutral (return) conductor
The earth (protective) conductor
The switched line conductor
The strapper from the switch

questions.stem: Why is the earth conductor connected to the earth terminal of a metal switch box?
options: So that the switch works more quickly when pressed
So that the light is brighter when it is switched on
So that less current flows in the line conductor
So a fault makes the protective device operate

questions.stem: In a two-way switching circuit, which terminals on each switch take the two strapper (traveller) wires?
options: The common terminal on each switch, and nothing else
The earth terminal and the common terminal on each switch
Any two terminals at all, because the order does not matter
The two terminals that are not the common terminal

questions.stem: What does "correct polarity" mean in an installation?
options: Line, neutral and earth all go to the right terminals
Every circuit has the same colour of cable throughout
All the accessories face the same way on every wall
The neutral is switched so that the line is always live

questions.stem: In most wiring systems, what colour is used for the earth (protective) conductor?
options: Blue, or blue and white
Red, or red and black
Green, or green and yellow
Brown, or brown and grey

questions.stem: Why should a conductor be marked with coloured sleeving or tape where its colour does not show its use?
options: To make the box look neat and colourful
So that anyone can tell what the conductor is for
To stop the conductor carrying too much current
Because sleeving makes the terminal screw grip better

questions.stem: Why are metal water pipes bonded to the main earthing terminal?
options: So that the pipes carry the neutral current back
To keep metal parts at the same voltage in a fault
To stop the water inside the pipes from getting hot
So that the pipes can be used as the circuit earth

questions.stem: After a new circuit is installed, which test proves that the earth conductor is joined all the way to each point?
options: An insulation resistance test between cores
A live voltage test at each outlet in turn
A continuity test of the earth conductor
A test of the breaker's trip time on fault

questions.stem: Why is an insulation resistance test done before a new installation is switched on?
options: To check there is no breakdown or short between conductors
To find out how much the electricity will cost each month
To check that the lamps are the right wattage for the room
To prove that the earth conductor is joined at every point

questions.stem: Who should carry out the tests on a new installation before it is switched on?
options: Any member of the public who owns a tester
The customer, using a plug-in tester
The trainee alone, without anyone checking
A competent person, using approved instruments

questions.stem: Which tool should you use to tighten the small terminal screws in an accessory?
options: Long-nose pliers gripped on the screw head
A hammer and a small centre punch
A screwdriver that fits the screw head
An adjustable spanner set to the screw

questions.stem: Why do electricians use screwdrivers with insulated handles and shafts?
options: So that they can be used on live conductors safely
So that they are lighter to carry in the tool bag
So that the screws are tightened more firmly
As an extra safeguard; you still never work live

questions.stem: When fitting an outlet to its box, how should the conductors be arranged?
options: Pulled tight so they cannot move in the box
Folded neatly into the box, without strain
Cut very short so there is no spare at all
Wrapped around the fixing screws to hold them

questions.stem: Where should cable joints (connections) be made in an installation?
options: Inside a box or enclosure that can be reached
Anywhere along the run, wrapped in insulating tape
Inside the wall plaster, where nobody can touch them
In the middle of a conduit run, between two boxes

questions.stem: Twist-on (wire nut) connectors are used to join conductors in a box. What should you follow?
options: The maker's guide for the number and size of wires
Use any size, as long as tape is wrapped around it
Twist the connector until the insulation splits
Fit it over bare ends that stick out past the connector

questions.stem: In a radial circuit, how are the outlets connected?
options: In a loop that starts and ends at the board
One after another along a cable from the board
Each to its own breaker, with no shared cable
In series, so current flows through each one

questions.stem: When connecting a new circuit into a dead, isolated distribution board, where does its line conductor go?
options: To the neutral bar, with the other neutrals
To the earth bar, beside the main earth
Straight onto the incoming supply terminals
To the outgoing terminal of its circuit breaker

questions.stem: Why should the cables inside a distribution board be dressed (laid) neatly?
options: So that the board uses up as much cable as possible
So the board's cover can be left off while it is used
So each circuit can be traced, and heat can escape
So the cables are pulled tight across the busbars

questions.stem: Before the cover is fitted on a finished board, what should you look for?
options: That every cable is the same length inside
Loose strands, bare copper and loose terminals
That the circuit labels have been left off
That the breakers are all switched on

questions.stem: Why must each circuit breaker be labelled with the circuit it controls?
options: So the customer knows what each breaker costs
So the breakers can be fitted in any order you like
So the right circuit can be isolated quickly
So the board looks the same as the drawing

questions.stem: What should you do with copper off-cuts and stripped sheath at the end of the day?
options: Collect them for recycling or the right waste bin
Leave them up in the ceiling space for the next job
Sweep them into the floor drain outside
Push them inside the board for later

questions.stem: When should a locked-off circuit be switched back on?
options: As soon as the first new cable has been connected up
Whenever anyone on the site asks for the power back on
When the tag has faded so much that nobody can read it
When work is done and checked, by whoever locked it off

questions.stem: Why should power cables be kept apart from data and telephone cables?
options: To reduce interference and keep different voltages apart
Because data cables carry more current than power cables
So that the data cables can be used as earth conductors
Because power and data cables must be different colours

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Name the tool that squeezes a lug or ferrule onto the end of a conductor.
Name the long steel or nylon tape used to pull cables into a conduit.
In a single-phase circuit, which conductor carries the current back to the supply?
What is the name of the bar in a distribution board where all the circuit earth conductors are connected?
How many strapper (traveller) wires link two two-way switches?
What is the name of the small metal tube crimped onto the end of a stranded conductor before it goes into a terminal?

Name the instrument used to test the insulation resistance of a circuit.
In what unit is insulation resistance usually given?

What type of switch is fitted between two two-way switches so that one light can be controlled from three places?
Name the hand tool used to cut copper conductors cleanly to length.
On metric cable, in what unit is the conductor size (cross-sectional area) given?
What is the name of the check made by looking carefully at the installation before any tests are done?
On a Jamaican 110/220 V home supply, what is the voltage between one line conductor and the neutral?

essays.stem: Describe the full safe isolation procedure you would follow before connecting a new cable into an existing circuit.
essays.modelAnswer: I find the right circuit from the board schedule and tell the people who will lose power. I switch off the circuit breaker for that circuit, then lock it off with my own padlock and a lock-off device, and keep the key with me. I fit a danger tag with my name, the date and 'Do not switch on'. I check my approved voltage tester on a proving unit or a known live source to show that it works. Then, at the point where I will work, I test between line and neutral, line and earth, and neutral and earth. When all show no voltage, I check the tester again on the proving unit. Only then do I start work. I remember that the incoming terminals in the board can still be live. I never work live.
markingPoints: Identifies the circuit and informs the people affected
Switches off, locks off with own lock and keeps the key
Fits a filled-in danger tag
Proves the tester, tests between all conductors at the point of work, proves the tester again
Never works live; knows the board's incoming terminals stay live

essays.stem: Compare a sheathed cable system clipped to the surface with a cable-in-conduit system. Give two advantages of each, and say where you would use each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Clipped sheathed cable is quick and cheap to install, because the cable has its own outer sheath and only needs clips. It needs few tools and is light to carry. But it is easy to damage, so it is used where it is protected, such as in ceiling spaces, inside stud walls, or in rooms where it will not be knocked. Cable in conduit takes longer and costs more, because the conduit must be cut, bent and fixed before the cables are drawn in. Its advantages are that the cables are well protected from damage, and that circuits can be rewired or added later by drawing new cables in, without breaking walls. It is used in block walls and concrete, in workshops and commercial buildings, and anywhere cables could be damaged.
markingPoints: Sheathed cable: quick and cheap to install
Sheathed cable: light, few tools; used where it is protected
Conduit: good protection from damage
Conduit: can be rewired or added to later
Conduit used in block or concrete, workshops and commercial buildings

essays.stem: Describe how you would draw (pull) cables into a conduit run safely and without damaging them.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check that the conduit run is complete, with all bends, boxes and bushes fitted, and that the inside is clean and free of burrs. I make sure the number and size of cables will fit, as the drawing and code allow. I set the cable reels on a stand so that they turn freely and the cables do not twist. I push a fish tape through from one box to the next, tie the cables to it with the ends staggered, and tape them neatly so they pass through easily. One person feeds the cables in straight and untwisted while another pulls steadily. I pull from box to box using the draw-in points, without too much force. I leave enough cable at each box for the connections, and label each cable.
markingPoints: Checks the conduit is complete, clean and free of burrs
Keeps within the allowed number and size of cables
Uses free-turning reels so cables do not twist
Uses a fish tape with taped, staggered ends; feeds and pulls steadily box to box
Leaves enough cable for connections and labels the cables

essays.stem: Describe how to prepare and terminate a sheathed cable at an outlet, from stripping the sheath to fixing the outlet to its box.
essays.modelAnswer: With the circuit isolated and proved dead, I bring the cable into the box through a grommet or bush, with the sheath going just inside the box. I cut the cable to leave enough length to connect the outlet and fold it back in. I remove the outer sheath with a cable stripper, taking care not to cut the insulation of the cores. I strip each core to the length the terminal needs, so that no bare copper shows outside the terminal. If the earth conductor is bare, I fit earth sleeving. I connect line, neutral and earth to the correct terminals, tighten them to the maker's torque, and give each a gentle tug. I fold the conductors neatly into the box without strain, and fix the outlet level with the right screws.
markingPoints: Works only on an isolated circuit proved dead
Enters the box through a grommet with the sheath just inside
Strips sheath and cores without damage, to the right length
Correct terminals, tightened, earth sleeved, tug-tested
Folds conductors neatly and fixes the outlet level

essays.stem: Explain how a one-way lighting circuit is connected, from the distribution board to the switch and the lamp, and why the switch must be in the line conductor.
essays.modelAnswer: The line conductor leaves the circuit breaker in the distribution board and goes to the lighting point or a junction box. From there, the line goes to one terminal of the one-way switch. The other switch terminal sends the switched line back to the lamp holder. The neutral goes from the neutral bar straight to the lamp holder, and the earth conductor goes from the earth bar to the switch box and the light fitting. When the switch is closed, current flows along the line, through the lamp and back on the neutral. The switch must be in the line conductor so that, when it is off, the lamp holder and fitting are not live. If the switch were in the neutral, the lamp would go off but the holder would stay live, and a person changing the lamp could get a shock.
markingPoints: Line from the breaker to the switch
Switched line from the switch to the lamp holder
Neutral straight to the lamp holder; earth to the switch box and fitting
Explains the current path when the switch is on
Switch in the line so the lamp holder is dead when off

essays.stem: Explain how two two-way switches control one light from two places, and describe the conductors used between the switches and the lamp.
essays.modelAnswer: Each two-way switch has a common terminal and two other terminals. The line conductor goes to the common terminal of the first switch. Two strapper (traveller) conductors link the two other terminals of the first switch to the two other terminals of the second switch. The common terminal of the second switch sends the switched line to the lamp, and the neutral goes straight from the supply to the lamp. Each switch joins its common terminal to one strapper or the other. When both switches are joined to the same strapper, the circuit is complete and the lamp is on. If either switch is turned, the path is broken and the lamp goes off. An earth conductor goes to both switch boxes and the light. North American catalogues call these switches 'three-way' switches.
markingPoints: Each switch has a common and two strapper terminals
Line to the common of the first switch; two strappers between the switches
Switched line from the second common to the lamp; neutral straight to the lamp
Explains how either switch turns the lamp on or off
Earth to both switch boxes and the light

essays.stem: Explain why the metal parts of an installation are earthed and bonded, and how the earth conductor is connected at accessories and at the board.
essays.modelAnswer: If a line conductor touches a metal box, a light fitting or an appliance case, that metal can become live and give a deadly shock. Earthing gives the fault current a low-resistance path back to the supply, so a large current flows and the circuit breaker or fuse operates quickly and cuts off the supply. Bonding links metal water pipes and other metal services to the main earthing terminal, so that all metal parts stay at nearly the same voltage during a fault. At each accessory, the circuit earth conductor is sleeved where it is bare and connected to the earth terminal of the accessory and of any metal box. At the board, each circuit earth goes to the earth bar, which is joined to the main earth.
markingPoints: A fault can make exposed metal live and cause a shock
Earthing gives a low-resistance path so the protective device operates
Bonding keeps metal parts at nearly the same voltage
At accessories: earth sleeved and connected to accessory and metal box
At the board: circuit earths to the earth bar, joined to the main earth

essays.stem: Describe the checks and tests that should be done on a newly installed circuit before it is switched on, and say who should do them.
essays.modelAnswer: First a visual inspection is done: correct cable types and sizes, no damage, cables supported, accessories fixed, terminals tight, earth sleeving fitted, covers on and circuits labelled. Then dead tests are done with approved instruments while the circuit is isolated. A continuity test proves that the earth conductor is joined from the board to every point. Polarity is checked, so that every switch and protective device is in the line conductor and lamp holder centre contacts are on the line. An insulation resistance test checks that there is no breakdown between conductors or to earth. The results are written down. Only a competent person, such as a qualified electrician or the instructor, carries out the tests, and the installation must be inspected and approved as the law requires before it is connected.
markingPoints: Visual inspection first, with examples of what is checked
Continuity of the earth conductor to every point
Polarity check
Insulation resistance test
Done by a competent person, results recorded, approved before connection

essays.stem: Describe what good workmanship looks like inside a finished outlet box and inside a distribution board, and say why it matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Inside a good outlet box, the sheath goes just inside the box through a grommet, the cores are stripped to the right length with no bare copper showing, the earth is sleeved, and every terminal is tight. The conductors are folded in neatly without strain, and the outlet is fixed level. Inside a good distribution board, the cables enter through the right glands or grommets, the conductors are dressed neatly along the sides, there are no loose strands, and each circuit's line, neutral and earth can be traced. Every breaker is labelled, and a circuit chart is fixed inside the door. Good workmanship matters because loose or damaged connections can overheat and cause fires or shocks, and because a neat board is easier and safer to test, maintain and fault-find.
markingPoints: Outlet box: sheath entry, correct strip lengths, earth sleeved, tight terminals
Outlet box: conductors folded neatly, outlet fixed level
Board: conductors dressed neatly, no loose strands, circuits traceable
Board: breakers labelled and a circuit chart fitted
Why: prevents overheating, fire and shock; easier testing and maintenance

essays.stem: Explain the things that affect the choice of cable type and size for a new circuit.
essays.modelAnswer: The cable must safely carry the current of the load, so the size is chosen for the full load current and must suit the rating of the circuit breaker that protects it. Long runs cause voltage drop, so a larger cable may be needed to keep the voltage at the far end high enough. The way the cable is installed also matters: cables in conduit, covered by insulation, bunched together or in hot places such as roof spaces cannot carry as much current, so they may need a larger size. The type of cable depends on the place: sheathed cable for dry, protected places, cable in conduit for block walls, and suitable armoured or outdoor cable for buried or outside runs. The cable must also suit the voltage, 110 V or 220 V. The final choice is taken from the drawing and the code.
markingPoints: Load current and the rating of the protective device
Voltage drop on long runs
Installation method, grouping and heat
Place and conditions decide the cable type
Final choice follows the drawing and the code

practical1.title: Wire one-way and two-way lighting circuits on a training board
practical1.brief: On a training board that is not connected to any supply, the group installs, terminates and connects a one-way switch controlling one lamp holder, and two two-way switches controlling a second lamp holder, both fed from one lighting circuit breaker in a small training distribution board. Use sheathed cable clipped to the board, or single cables in the conduit already fixed to the board, as the assessor directs. Before work starts, each member in turn practises the safe isolation steps on the board's isolator, using the proving unit. Share the wiring so that every member strips and terminates at least two accessories while the assessor watches. When the wiring is complete, the group makes dead checks with a continuity tester: earth continuity to every point, and that each switch is in the line conductor and works the lamp holder it should. The group never switches the board on. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the work is finished and the area is clean.
materials: Training board with a small distribution board, two lamp holders, one one-way switch and two two-way switches, with boxes
Sheathed lighting cable, or single cables for the board's conduit, as the assessor directs
Cable clips, grommets and earth sleeving
Insulated screwdrivers, side cutters, cable stripper and wire strippers
Continuity tester or multimeter, and a proving unit
Lock-off device, padlock and danger tag
photos: The board's isolator locked off and tagged, with the tester being proved
Cables run and clipped (or drawn in) before termination
A one-way switch box with conductors terminated, before the switch is fixed
A two-way switch box showing the common and strapper terminals
A lamp holder terminated, showing the switched line and neutral
The distribution board with the circuit terminated and labelled
A continuity check being made with the tester
The finished board and the clean work area
checklist: Carried out the safe isolation steps in the right order before touching the board
Ran and fixed cables neatly, with grommets where cables enter boxes
Stripped sheath and cores without damage, to the right length, with no bare copper showing
Fitted earth sleeving and connected the earth at every accessory and box
Connected switches in the line conductor, with strappers on the correct two-way terminals
Tightened every terminal and gave each conductor a gentle tug test
Made the dead continuity checks correctly and recorded the results
Labelled the circuit and left the board tidy with covers fitted
safety: The training board must not be connected to any supply during the task; the group never switches it on
Practise safe isolation before starting: switch off, lock off, tag, and prove dead with a tester proved before and after
Use insulated tools in good condition, and strip cable away from your body
Wear safety glasses when cutting conductors and fixing clips
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Install and terminate a radial outlet circuit and a 220 V appliance circuit
practical2.brief: On a training bay that is not connected to any supply, the group installs a 110 V radial outlet circuit feeding three outlets, and a 220 V circuit from a two-pole breaker to a two-pole isolator for an appliance such as a water heater, using the cable types and routes on the assessor's drawing. Terminate the cables at the outlets, at the isolator and in the training distribution board (outgoing breaker terminals, neutral bar and earth bar). Each member terminates at least one outlet or the isolator, and makes at least one board connection while the assessor watches. Then make dead checks with a continuity tester: earth continuity to each point, and correct polarity at each outlet and at the isolator. Label each circuit and fill in a simple circuit chart. The group never switches the bay on. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Training bay with a training distribution board (not connected to any supply)
One single-pole breaker and one two-pole breaker of the type the drawing shows
Three outlets with boxes, and one two-pole isolator
Cable of the type and size shown on the drawing, with clips or the conduit already fitted
Grommets, earth sleeving, ferrules and a crimp tool
Insulated hand tools, cable stripper and wire strippers
Continuity tester or multimeter, proving unit, lock-off device, padlock and danger tag
photos: The bay isolator locked off and tagged before work
Cables installed between the board and each point
An outlet terminated before it is fixed to its box
The distribution board with both circuits terminated and dressed neatly
A polarity or continuity check being made
The completed circuit chart and labels
The finished bay and the clean work area
checklist: Carried out the safe isolation steps in the right order before starting
Followed the drawing for cable type, route and connection points
Terminated outlets with line, neutral and earth on the correct terminals
Connected the 220 V circuit correctly to both poles of the breaker and the isolator
Made board connections to the right breaker, neutral bar and earth bar, neatly dressed
Tightened all terminals and tug-tested every conductor
Made continuity and polarity checks on the dead circuit and recorded the results
Labelled the circuits, filled in the circuit chart and left the area tidy
safety: The training bay must not be connected to any supply; the group never switches it on
Practise safe isolation first: switch off, lock off, tag, and prove dead with a tester proved before and after
Use insulated tools in good condition, and keep the floor clear of cable off-cuts
Wear safety glasses when cutting and stripping conductors
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
